record.title: ActGov reports benchmark reductions in indirect prompt-injection success through per-action authorization checks
record.summary: A September 2026 preprint introduces ActGov, which checks each proposed tool call against a task-scoped policy before execution. The authors report lower indirect prompt-injection success on AgentDojo and AgentDyn across four model backends, with task utility retained to varying degrees. Their cross-domain transfer test also shows severe over-restriction: an AgentDojo-trained policy has 0.100 clean-task utility on AgentDyn versus 0.767 without defense. These are paper-reported benchmark results, not independent reproduction or evidence of deployment effectiveness.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors propose an offline policy-generation stage with Z3 checking and a deterministic runtime monitor that intercepts each candidate tool call before external execution.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On the displayed AgentDojo and AgentDyn test splits, the authors report ActGov attack-success rates from 0 to 0.7% across four model backends, with varying reductions in task utility.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In cross-domain policy transfer, the authors report zero attack success but severe over-restriction; an AgentDojo-trained policy has 0.100 clean utility on AgentDyn compared with 0.767 for no defense.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The results do not establish that the policy abstraction or semantic extraction is reliable in open-world deployments, nor that attack reductions generalize beyond these benchmark tasks and assumptions.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of the AgentDojo/AgentDyn split or author-reported attack-success and task-utility values was performed.
Evaluation assumes trusted user tasks, an immutable enforcement layer, and complete pre-execution interception; open-world tools and unseen task domains are not established.
Cross-domain policy transfer preserves low reported attack success through severe conservatism, including 0.100 clean utility on AgentDyn for an AgentDojo-trained policy.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported results generalize, per-action authorization checks could reduce indirect prompt-injection risk in long-running tool agents while preserving useful actions. The paper reports strong in-benchmark attack-rate reductions but severe utility loss under cross-domain policy transfer, so the result is notable engineering evidence rather than a general security guarantee.
limitations: All attack-success and utility measurements are author-reported; the research desk did not run code or reproduce results.
The threat model trusts the user task and enforcement layer and assumes every external action passes through pre-execution validation.
Policy abstraction depends on finite records and semantic extraction; errors in mapping runtime context can affect enforcement.
The main evidence comes from two benchmark suites and specific task splits; cross-domain transfer shows severe utility loss.
The strongest policy-generation setting uses human review, so it does not demonstrate fully autonomous policy synthesis in that setting.
brief.summary: A September 2026 preprint introduces ActGov, which checks each proposed tool call against a task-scoped policy before execution. The authors report lower indirect prompt-injection success on AgentDojo and AgentDyn across four model backends, with task utility retained to varying degrees. Their cross-domain transfer test also shows severe over-restriction: an AgentDojo-trained policy has 0.100 clean-task utility on AgentDyn versus 0.767 without defense. These are paper-reported benchmark results, not independent reproduction or evidence of deployment effectiveness.

technical.claimed_result: On AgentDyn, the authors report ActGov attack success rates of 0.004–0.007 across Qwen3.6-Flash, MiniMax-M2.5, DeepSeek-V4-Pro and GPT-4o mini. On AgentDojo they report 0.000 for all four backends in the displayed test split. Task-completion utility declines in some configurations. Cross-domain policies yield 0.000 ASR in both transfer directions but can sharply restrict benign tasks; an AgentDojo-trained policy tested on AgentDyn has 0.100 clean utility versus 0.767 without defense.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected arXiv v2 paper reports the framework, benchmark setup and tabulated results. the research desk did not execute the code or independently reproduce the measurements; the attack and utility outcomes remain author-reported.
technical.mechanism: ActGov separates offline policy generation from deterministic runtime enforcement. An LLM proposes policy rules from tool specifications, benign traces and attacks; Z3 checks candidate policies against predefined invariants. At runtime a monitor maps a proposed action and context into finite semantic records and allows it only when it passes the task permissions and policy rules.
technical.regime: Indirect prompt-injection tests on AgentDojo (629 security test cases) and AgentDyn (560 security test cases), with four model backends. The main evaluation uses equal training/test splits. The strongest policy setting uses GPT-5.5 as policy proposer for 10 refinement rounds with human review; a separate scalability evaluation removes that review and uses five automated iterations.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper compares against no defense and CaMeL, Progent, DRIFT and ACE. It reports attack-success and clean/attacked task-completion metrics; cross-domain transfer substantially reduces utility despite low attack success.

brief.title: ActGov reports benchmark reductions in indirect prompt-injection success through per-action authorization checks
brief.why_it_matters: ActGov tests a concrete security boundary: authorization is checked at each proposed external action rather than delegated to the model's judgment. The paper's held-out benchmark results make that mechanism worth tracking, while the cross-domain utility collapse shows that low attack success can result from blocking legitimate work. Deployment value depends on whether policy coverage and semantic extraction generalize beyond the tested task splits.
